extracted.intended_audience: policy makers, IP office staff, IP practitioners, researchers and analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and interpreting WIPO's definitions, metrics and statistical indicators used to describe patenting activity (applications, grants, families, resident/non-resident status, technology fields, and related procedural concepts) for comparative and analytical work on patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent (patentability criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of exclusive rights granted by law to applicants for inventions that are new, non-obvious and commercially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent is valid for a limited period (generally 20 years) and in return the applicant must disclose the invention so others skilled in the art can replicate it. The patent system is designed to encourage innovation by providing time-limited exclusive rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model (eligibility and characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: A special form of patent right granted by a state or jurisdiction for a fixed period of time with slightly different terms and conditions than normal patents (including a shorter term of protection and less stringent patentability requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also known as 'petty patents', 'short-term patents' or 'innovation patents' in some countries; utility model data are reported separately from invention patents in WIPO statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent family (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of interrelated patent applications filed at one or more offices to protect the same invention, interlinked by one or more of: priority claim, PCT national phase entry, continuation, continuation-in-part, internal priority, and addition or division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO’s patent family definition includes only families associated with patent applications for inventions and excludes those associated with utility model applications. Patent family indicators are used to approximate the actual number of unique inventions by reducing double-counting across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-oriented patent family (quality indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent family that has at least one filing office different from the office of the applicant’s country of origin (some foreign-oriented families may include only one filing office if applicant files directly abroad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign-oriented patent families are usually considered to be of higher quality and value because filing in multiple jurisdictions is costly and applicants tend to be selective; such families improve cross-country comparisons by reducing home bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resident application (statistical classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: For statistical purposes, a resident application is an application filed with the IP office of, or acting for, the state or jurisdiction in which the first named applicant in the application is resident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resident applications are sometimes called domestic applications; resident grants/registrations are those issued on the basis of resident applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-resident application (statistical classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: For statistical purposes, a non-resident (or foreign) application refers to an application filed with the IP office of a state or jurisdiction in which the first named applicant is not domiciled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-resident application counts are used to characterise cross-border filing flows to particular offices and to compute shares of resident vs non-resident activity at offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin (country or region) of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The country or territory of residence of the first named applicant in the application (for statistical purposes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Origin data can be reported either as absolute counts or equivalent counts; origin data are partial/incomplete because some offices report aggregate totals without origin breakdown, and filings at regional offices may distort origin totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications filed abroad / abroad filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications filed by applicants at foreign offices (i.e., outside the residence of the first named applicant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abroad filings are considered to reflect patents of high value (monetary, strategic, etc.). They are costly and time-consuming and thus serve as an indicator for higher-value inventions and improve cross-country comparisons by reducing domestic bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent applications (office-level counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts of patent applications received by IP offices in a given year, often disaggregated into resident and non-resident components and ranked by office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office-level application numbers reflect both domestic innovation and cross-border filing behaviour; comparisons across offices should account for differences in scope (e.g., invention patents vs utility models) and reporting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents granted (grant counts) and examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts of patents issued by offices after formal and substantive examination; the procedure for granting a patent varies between offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application data for a given year should not be compared directly with grant data from the same year because grants reflect examination capacity and procedural delays; differences across offices in grants depend on examination capacity and procedural delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent family size / geographical coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of offices at which a patent family is filed; single-office vs multi-office family classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A larger family size indicates wider geographical coverage. Around 85% of families (2019–2021) were single-office; Chinese-origin families are disproportionately single-office. Family size varies by origin and reflects market size and multinational presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-to-GDP ratio (resident patents per unit GDP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resident patent applications per USD 100 billion GDP (used to adjust patenting activity for economy size).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for cross-country comparison of patenting intensity; top-ranking economies by this ratio are typically high-income with high R&D expenditure. Trends can reflect resident filings growth relative to GDP growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-to-population ratio (resident patents per million population)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resident patent applications adjusted per million population to measure per-capita patenting intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a view similar to patent-to-GDP but highlights differences due to population size; composition of top origins may differ slightly from GDP-adjusted ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-field classification (IPC-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment of published patent applications to technology fields based on International Patent Classification (IPC) symbols and WIPO field mappings (e.g., computer technology, electrical machinery, medical technology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPC-to-field mapping is not always clear-cut; WIPO provides IPC-based definitions for fields and warns that while not perfect, the definitions capture the vast majority of related patents. Field shares and growth rates (e.g., computer technology share and growth) are reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patent families to count unique inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting patent families rather than raw application counts to approximate the number of unique inventions and avoid double counting when aggregating across jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent-family-based indicators have a time lag of up to three years but reduce duplication inherent in simple application tallies; WIPO notes trade-offs between timeliness and de-duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority date (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing date of the application on the basis of which priority is claimed (Paris Convention right of priority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority allows applicants to claim the earlier filing date in subsequent filings made within the priority period (12 months for patents), which is central to establishing novelty/priority among competing filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication date (definition and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The date on which an IP application is disclosed to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On publication date the subject matter becomes prior art and can affect novelty and inventive-step assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending patent application (status definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application filed with a patent office for which a patent has yet to be granted or refused and which has not been withdrawn; in jurisdictions requiring a request for examination, pending may mean the request has been received or not yet decided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pending status is relevant for measuring backlog, timeliness of examination, and comparisons across offices with differing procedural triggers for examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT System and national phase (procedural route)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT System facilitates acquisition of patent rights across many jurisdictions by providing an international phase (search and possible preliminary examination) followed by national phase entry in designated countries or regions where protection is sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PCT simplifies multiple filings but national/regional patent offices retain final patentability decisions; PCT national-phase entries are one way patent families are linked across offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paris Convention – right of priority (procedural rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle enabling an IP applicant to claim priority of an earlier application filed up to 12 months previously for patents (and utility models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention underpins the priority mechanism used to construct patent families and to determine priority dates when assessing novelty and inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional application/grant (definition and effect on statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application filed with or granted by an IP office having regional jurisdiction over more than one country (e.g., EPO, ARIPO, OAPI, EAPO, EUIPO, BOIP, GCC Patent Office).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional filings/grants affect origin and office counts because a single regional filing can cover multiple countries, leading to lower origin counts for countries using regional systems; this should be accounted for in cross-country comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance / Renewal (keeping IP rights in force)
rubrics_metrics.description: An act by the applicant to keep an IP grant/registration valid (in force), primarily by paying the required fee to the IP office; patents, utility models and industrial designs can be maintained only for a limited number of years, while trademarks can be renewed indefinitely in many jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to pay maintenance/renewal fees leads to lapse; maintenance behaviour can be an indicator of the economic value of IP rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification systems referenced (IPC, Locarno, Nice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of internationally harmonized classification schemes to group patents, designs and trademarks: IPC for patents, Locarno for industrial designs, Nice Classification for goods and services in trademark registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO maps IPC symbols to technology fields for analysis and notes that correspondence between IPC symbols and technology fields is not always clear-cut; annexes provide IPC symbol lists for specific technology definitions (e.g., energy-related fields).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of office/region shares and trends for interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting and interpreting shares of world totals (e.g., an office's share of world patent applications, or a region's share such as Asia receiving ~68.7% of applications in 2023).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO advises considering long-term trends, composition changes (e.g., growth in resident filings in China), and the influence of office practices when interpreting shares and trends across years and offices.
